subject: Throughput & streaming window qualifiers — next steps
messages:
From: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>
To: Sam Tu <sam@velociti.ai>, Nina Park <nina@velociti.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 29 May 2027 15:02:00 -0700
Subject: Throughput & streaming window qualifiers — next steps

Thanks for the sync today — short recap and concrete asks so we can size the pilot platform correctly. Key outcomes:

- Velociti has two primary request classes: short conversational queries (chat) and long-document summarization (batch/streaming).
- Streaming is required for the long-doc summarization path (server-streaming tokens to the client). We need clarity on parallel streams per user and expected steady vs peak behavior.

Actions we need from you (Sam/Nina):
1) Provide a 30–60 minute token-level trace (sample) from a typical 1-hour window that includes both request classes. If possible, include timestamps for request start/end and token counts.
2) Confirm latency SLOs: you mentioned p95 ~200ms for chat and p95 ~3s for streaming first-chunk — confirm.
3) Call out peak burst characteristics: how many QPS sustained for 1–5 minutes vs steady baseline.

What we’ll provide back by EOD Monday: a model of tokens/sec -> QPS conversions, a baseline sizing (recommended GPU pool + concurrency), and a suggested canary plan for the pilot.

Quick note on token/QPS mapping we’ll use (example):
- short chat: avg 80 tokens, target p95 200ms -> map to ~12 QPS per 1k tokens/sec (we’ll show calculations).
- long-doc stream: avg 1.4k tokens with streaming; these create long-lived token emission (tokens/sec matters more than QPS).

Attachment: placeholder for sample token schema we asked for (I’ll drop a template if you don’t have one).

Thanks — Mina
Mina Haddad
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Sam Tu <sam@velociti.ai>

Subject: Re: Throughput & streaming window qualifiers — next steps

Thanks Mina — good summary. Attaching a 1-hour trace (anonymized) and a short notes file that explains the event types. Quick clarifications below.

What’s in the trace: 1 hour (2027-05-26 11:00–12:00 local), ~28k total requests. Two classes:
- CHAT: ~23k requests, avg tokens/request = 78, median latency on our client call = 160ms.
- DOC_STREAM: ~5k requests, avg input tokens = 1,400, server streams output tokens over ~4–10s window.

Peak behavior: we see a 5-minute crest where QPS jumped to ~600 overall (mostly chat), baseline steady QPS ~80. Typical concurrency for streaming sessions: clients open 2–4 concurrent streams per user (depending on UI).

Latency SLOs: we aim for p95 <= 200ms for chat, p95 <= 3s to first chunk for streaming — those are what we’d like to test.

Attached: velocii_1h_token_trace.json (sanitized)

Sam
Sam Tu
Lead Product, Velociti

From: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Throughput & streaming window qualifiers — next steps

Perfect — thanks for the trace, Sam. I digested the file and sketched an initial conversion and a couple of sizing scenarios. High level:

1) Tokens/sec -> QPS mapping (two request archetypes)
   - CHAT: avg 78 tokens/request -> if a GPU pool can sustain 200k tokens/sec, that maps to ~2,564 chat QPS at nominal token cost (200000 / 78).
   - DOC_STREAM: streaming path emits ~500 tokens/sec while a session is active (depends on model + decoding). A single long-doc session therefore consumes ~500 t/s during active emission.

2) Peak vs steady interpretation (from your 1-hour):
   - Baseline: ~80 QPS (mostly chat) -> ~6.2k tokens/sec (80 * 78).
   - 5-min crest: 600 QPS (chat-heavy) -> ~46.8k tokens/sec. If doc-stream is active concurrently, add N * 500 t/s per active stream.

3) Sizing scenarios (quick):
   - Minimal pilot: target baseline + 2x crest headroom = design for ~100k tokens/sec (covers crest + 2–3 concurrent doc streams).
   - Production-ish: 250k tokens/sec with streaming-optimized batch/kv caching and 95th percentile latency target.

4) Proposed concrete next steps from Redwood:
   - We’ll produce a sizing spreadsheet (attached) showing tokens/sec -> QPS -> estimated GPU vCPU and expected p95/p99 latencies under continuous batching vs pure streaming paths.
   - Recommend a canary plan: start with 4 x A100-style nodes reserved for the pilot with autoscaling to +2 nodes on crest detection; streaming sessions pinned to a streaming-optimized pool to avoid head-of-line blocking.
   - Ask you to provide a 10-minute high-traffic sample (crest window) and mark how many simultaneous long-doc streams were active during that time.

Attachment: velociti_sizing_estimate_v2.xlsx (spreadsheet, 48KB)

I’ll follow up with a short slide that contains the math and the suggested guardrails (caching TTLs, batch windows, concurrency caps) so you can share with your infra team.

Are you available Monday morning for a 30-min follow-up to confirm the canary plan?

— Mina
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 30 May 2027 09:10:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Throughput & streaming window qualifiers — next steps

Adding a quick internal note — I reviewed Mina’s sizing and agree with the streaming-isolated pool approach. Two asks for the Monday call:

1) We should confirm the p99 latency objective for chat (is 400ms acceptable as a fallback under crest?).
2) Propose we offer a streaming-only configuration that routes long-doc sessions to a quantized model variant to reduce tokens/sec by ~20% (we’ll show quantization tradeoffs).

I’ll be on the call Monday 9:00am PT if that works.

- Karthik
